positions/social-gospel/oneLine: The gospel aims to transform not only individuals but social structures, so Christians must work to Christianise economic and political life in line with the kingdom of God.
positions/social-gospel/coreClaims/0: The kingdom of God, the centre of Jesus’ preaching, is a social reality to be realised progressively in history.
positions/social-gospel/coreClaims/1: Sin is embodied in "super-personal forces" such as exploitative economic systems, not only individual acts.
positions/social-gospel/coreClaims/2: Salvation includes redeeming social institutions: labour rights, fair wages, housing, public health.
positions/social-gospel/coreClaims/3: The Hebrew prophets and Jesus summon the Church to justice for the poor.
positions/social-gospel/origin: Christian Socialists in Britain (F. D. Maurice, Charles Kingsley, 1848) and American Protestants responding to industrialisation (Washington Gladden, Richard Ely, Josiah Strong) laid foundations; Walter Rauschenbusch, a Baptist pastor in New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, gave it classic form (Christianity and the Social Crisis, 1907; A Theology for the Social Gospel, 1917). Charles Sheldon’s novel In His Steps (1896) popularised "What would Jesus do?". The Federal Council of Churches adopted a Social Creed (1908). Parallels: Leo XIII’s Rerum Novarum (1891) and, in Japan, Toyohiko Kagawa.
positions/social-gospel/strongestArgumen: It recovers the prophetic and kingdom dimensions of Scripture that individualistic piety neglected.
It addressed real suffering (child labour, slums, 12-hour days) and achieved concrete reforms.
It influenced later movements, including civil rights, through figures such as Martin Luther King Jr.
positions/social-gospel/strongestObjecti: Fundamentalists and evangelicals charged that it replaced personal conversion and the atonement with social reform, tying it to theological liberalism.
Reinhold Niebuhr (Moral Man and Immoral Society, 1932) criticised its optimism about human nature and progress.
Some leaders shared racial and imperial assumptions of their era (e.g. Josiah Strong’s Anglo-Saxon triumphalism) and largely ignored racial injustice.
positions/social-gospel/responses/0: Rauschenbusch insisted on personal regeneration and wrote prayers of deep piety; he saw social and individual salvation as complementary.
positions/social-gospel/responses/1: Later evangelical statements (Lausanne Covenant, 1974, paragraph 5) reaffirmed social responsibility as part of Christian duty, partly vindicating its concerns.
positions/social-gospel/consequences/0: Shaped mainline Protestant social activism and ecumenical bodies (Federal Council of Churches, WCC).
positions/social-gospel/consequences/1: Contributed to Progressive Era reforms and the New Deal.
positions/social-gospel/consequences/2: Deepened the fundamentalist–modernist split, with evangelicals long suspicious of "social" Christianity.
positions/social-gospel/consequences/3: Fed into the civil rights movement and later liberation theologies.
positions/montanism/oneLine: The promised Paraclete was speaking afresh through the prophets Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla, calling the Church to stricter discipline and readiness for Christ’s coming.
positions/montanism/coreClaims/0: The Paraclete promised in John 14–16 now speaks directly through new prophets, completing the revelation of discipline (not of doctrine).
positions/montanism/coreClaims/1: Prophecy may come in ecstasy, with the prophet speaking in the first person as God.
positions/montanism/coreClaims/2: Christians should fast more strictly, refuse second marriage and not flee persecution.
positions/montanism/coreClaims/3: The heavenly Jerusalem would descend at Pepuza in Phrygia.
positions/montanism/coreClaims/4: Women may be prophets and, in later Montanist communities, hold clerical office.
positions/montanism/keyTexts/4: Tertullian, On Monogamy; On Fasting; On Flight in Persecution
positions/montanism/origin: Began in Phrygia (central Asia Minor) around 156–172 (sources differ) when the recent convert Montanus began prophesying ecstatically at Ardabau, joined by Priscilla (Prisca) and Maximilla. It spread to Rome, Gaul and North Africa, where Tertullian embraced it c.207. Its own name was "the New Prophecy".
positions/montanism/proponentsOther/4: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity is often thought to reflect New Prophecy sympathies (debated)
positions/montanism/strongestArguments/0: The New Testament promises continuing prophecy until Christ’s return (Acts 2:17; 1 Cor 13:8–12), and the second-century Church still had prophets (Didache 11; Irenaeus).
positions/montanism/strongestArguments/1: Its morality was rigorous and its doctrine of God orthodox; Tertullian’s Trinitarian theology was written as a Montanist.
positions/montanism/strongestArguments/2: It resisted the growing domestication of the Spirit by bishops and the laxity of a settling Church.
positions/montanism/strongestArguments/3: It recognised women’s prophetic ministry in line with Acts 2 and 21:9.
positions/montanism/strongestObjections/: Ecstatic, first-person speech "as God" broke with the tradition of prophets who spoke in their right mind (1 Cor 14:32: "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets").
Its prophecies failed: Maximilla predicted wars and the end after her death, yet there was a long peace (Anonymous in Eusebius 5.16.19).
By claiming the Paraclete’s final revelation it relativised the apostolic deposit and implied a new authority above the bishops and Scripture.
Critics accused its leaders of financial exploitation and of encouraging needless martyrdom.
positions/montanism/responses/0: Montanists replied that the Paraclete added discipline, not doctrine, and that the "rule of faith" was unchanged (Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins 1).
positions/montanism/responses/1: Modern historians (Trevett, Tabbernee) argue that much early polemic was exaggerated, and that the movement was largely a conservative, rigorist renewal of older Asian prophetic Christianity.
positions/montanism/consequences/0: Prompted the first recorded church synods (Asia Minor, c.177) and helped push the Church towards a closed canon and episcopal control of prophecy.
positions/montanism/consequences/1: Contributed to suspicion of ecstatic prophecy and of women’s leadership in the catholic Church.
positions/montanism/consequences/2: Survived in Phrygia until suppressed by Justinian in the 6th century; John of Ephesus burned the relics of the founders at Pepuza (c.550).
positions/montanism/consequences/3: Became a perennial reference point: cessationists see it as the archetype of charismatic excess, while some Pentecostals see it as an unjustly suppressed renewal.
positions/cessationism/oneLine: The miraculous or "sign" gifts (prophecy, tongues, healings, miracles) were given to authenticate the apostles and complete Scripture, and ceased with the apostolic age.
positions/cessationism/coreClaims/0: Miraculous gifts functioned chiefly to authenticate new revelation and its messengers (2 Cor 12:12; Heb 2:3–4).
positions/cessationism/coreClaims/1: The apostles and prophets were the once-for-all foundation of the Church (Eph 2:20); with the canon complete, revelatory gifts are no longer needed.
positions/cessationism/coreClaims/2: Biblical miracles cluster around epochs of revelation (Moses, Elijah/Elisha, Christ and the apostles) rather than occurring evenly.
positions/cessationism/coreClaims/3: God still answers prayer and may heal providentially, but no one today possesses the gift of healing or infallible prophecy.
positions/cessationism/origin: Patristic observations that the gifts had become rare (Chrysostom, Augustine’s early writings) were turned into a doctrine by Reformation polemic against Catholic miracle claims and radical "enthusiasts": Calvin argued that new miracles were not needed to confirm the old gospel (Prefatory Address to the Institutes, 1536). John Owen and the Puritans developed it, and B. B. Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles (1918) gave the classic modern statement in reaction to faith-healing and early Pentecostalism.
positions/cessationism/strongestArgument: It protects the sufficiency and finality of Scripture: if prophecy continues, new revelation competes with the canon.
The New Testament itself presents apostolic signs as distinctive credentials ("the signs of an apostle", 2 Cor 12:12), not as universal equipment.
Modern tongues and prophecy, it argues, differ from the New Testament phenomena (known languages in Acts 2; infallible prophecy in the Old Testament standard of Deut 18).
Church history shows a marked decline of claimed sign-gifts after the apostolic era, and recurrent movements claiming them have often produced error and abuse.
positions/cessationism/strongestObjectio: No text explicitly says the gifts will cease before Christ returns; most commentators read "that which is perfect" (1 Cor 13:10) as the eschaton, when we see "face to face".
Patristic sources (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Augustine’s own later City of God 22.8) report continuing miracles; the decline was gradual and contested (Ruthven).
It fits poorly with widespread reports of healings and prophetic experience in the Global South, where most Christians now live.
Paul commands "forbid not to speak with tongues" and "desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy" (1 Cor 14:1, 39) without time limits.
positions/cessationism/responses/0: Cessationists reply that 1 Corinthians 13 is not their main argument; the foundational, authenticating role of the gifts is.
positions/cessationism/responses/1: Many distinguish their view ("the sign gifts ceased") from denying miracles: God remains free to heal in answer to prayer.
positions/cessationism/responses/2: They argue that the quality of modern phenomena, not their quantity, is decisive, and that much reported prophecy is fallible impression rather than New Testament prophecy.
positions/cessationism/consequences/0: Shaped the worship and expectations of most confessional Reformed and many Baptist and fundamentalist churches.
positions/cessationism/consequences/1: Fuelled early fundamentalist hostility to Pentecostalism (e.g. the World’s Christian Fundamentals Association’s 1928 resolution against it).
positions/cessationism/consequences/2: Continues in vigorous debate with continuationists in global evangelicalism (Strange Fire conference, 2013).
positions/continuationism/oneLine: All the gifts of the Spirit, including prophecy, tongues and healing, remain available to the Church until Christ returns, to be exercised in love and tested by Scripture.
positions/continuationism/coreClaims/0: The gifts are for "the common good" (1 Cor 12:7) and the building up of the Church in every age, not merely for authenticating apostles.
positions/continuationism/coreClaims/1: They will cease only "when that which is perfect is come", i.e. at Christ’s return (1 Cor 13:10–12).
positions/continuationism/coreClaims/2: New Testament prophecy is distinct from canonical Scripture and must be weighed (1 Thess 5:19–21; 1 Cor 14:29).
positions/continuationism/coreClaims/3: Spirit baptism normally occurs at conversion; tongues are one gift among many, not required evidence.
positions/continuationism/origin: The working assumption of the 2nd-century Church (Justin, Irenaeus) and never formally abandoned in Eastern Orthodoxy or Catholicism, where charisms and miracles of saints remain expected. Within Protestantism it was revived through Wesleyan, Holiness and Pentecostal currents and given academic articulation by evangelical scholars such as Wayne Grudem (The Gift of Prophecy, 1988), Gordon Fee and D. A. Carson (Showing the Spirit, 1987).
positions/continuationism/strongestArgum: It takes the New Testament’s instructions on gifts as addressed to the whole Church, not only to the first generation.
The burden of proof lies on cessationism, since no text explicitly limits the gifts to the apostolic era.
It coheres with documented miracle reports across history and today (Craig Keener’s two-volume survey, 2011).
It fosters expectant prayer and ministry in line with Jesus’ commission to heal and cast out demons.
positions/continuationism/strongestObjec: Cessationists argue that "fallible prophecy" is a novel category that undermines the seriousness of claiming "thus says the Lord".
Critics point to abuses, false prophecies and manipulative healing campaigns within continuationist movements.
Some argue that contemporary tongues are learned speech patterns rather than languages (linguistic studies, e.g. William Samarin, 1972).
positions/continuationism/responses/0: Continuationists reply that abuse of a gift calls for discernment, not prohibition (1 Thess 5:20–21).
positions/continuationism/responses/1: They argue that New Testament congregational prophecy was always subject to weighing and was never treated as canonical (1 Cor 14:29; Acts 21:4, 10–14).
positions/continuationism/responses/2: Paul calls some tongues "tongues of angels" (1 Cor 13:1) and treats them as prayer not necessarily in human languages (1 Cor 14:2, 14).
positions/continuationism/consequences/0: Allowed charismatic practice within Reformed and Baptist churches (e.g. Sovereign Grace Churches, New Frontiers).
positions/continuationism/consequences/1: Became the majority stance among evangelical scholars and most Global South churches.
positions/continuationism/consequences/2: Lowered barriers between evangelicals and Pentecostals/charismatics.
